source.title: Where Should I Spend My FLOPS? Efficiency Evaluations of Visual Pre-training Methods
source.authors: Skanda Koppula; Ya-Zhe Li; Evan Shelhamer; Andrew Jaegle; Nikhil Parthasarathy; Relja Arandjelović; João Carreira; Olivier J. H'enaff

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates visual pre-training across model sizes and compute budgets and reports downstream performance results in this new modality. It does not fit or test power laws for pre-training loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as context, but it does not measure held-out pre-training loss, fit power laws, or test whether small-run fits predict larger-run loss. Its own model-size and compute comparisons report downstream visual-task performance.
record.test_reason: The study compares the compute efficiency of visual pre-training methods. It uses downstream ADE20K and COCO accuracy plotted against pre-training FLOPs, for two ViT sizes and five datasets. It fits no scaling law, measures no pre-training loss, and makes no claim that downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. The ViT-B vs ViT-L comparison is a two-point, compute-matched allocation question on downstream accuracy, so it does not test V6. The authors cite Kaplan and Hoffmann only as context, noting the SSL size trend is 'similar to what is observed in language model scaling'. Power-law fitting is explicitly left as future work.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find large (up to 10x) differences in FLOP efficiency across visual pre-training methods, with supervised/CLIP and MAE on the efficiency frontier and SimCLR, BYOL and DINO below. They find strong sensitivity to dataset curation, which questions the assumption that SSL inherently scales to uncurated data. They urge reporting accuracy relative to compute, and leave power-law characterisation of the curves to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Visual pre-training experiments comparing compute-normalized downstream accuracy, rather than language-model held-out loss or power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative compute-efficiency of model sizes varies by pre-training method and compute budget; the small- and large-model curves intersect for most methods.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed pre-training FLOP budget on JFT, the smaller ViT-B gives better ADE20K segmentation than ViT-L for CLIP. For most SSL methods, the ViT-B and ViT-L efficiency curves cross.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In visual pre-training, the downstream-accuracy-optimal model size at fixed compute depends on the pre-training method.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 250K steps, larger pre-training datasets (JFT, ALIGN) often do not beat ImageNet-1K on ADE20K (Table 1) or COCO detection (Table 2). Only SimCLR improves consistently with dataset size. Dataset size is confounded with curation level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream transfer accuracy of visual SSL does not scale with pre-training dataset size when curation varies.

record.peer_reviewed: 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Workshop on Self-Supervised Learning (2022)
record.problems: The study measures downstream visual-task performance rather than held-out pre-training loss, and does not fit power laws or test extrapolation. The model-size comparisons are described partly in qualitative terms without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. The other figures and tables report visual-task efficiency or dataset comparisons, not additional results needed to assess the tested downstream-performance-with-scale version.

untested.parts: No held-out pre-training loss is measured.
No loss-optimal parameter/token allocation law. Only two model sizes are compared on downstream accuracy.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Vision models are trained, but no power-law form is fitted to any loss or accuracy curve.
No test of whether downstream accuracy is predictable from scale or pre-training loss.

missing.what: Dataset-size results: ADE20K mIoU and COCO mAP by pre-training dataset for four SSL methods. These would be needed if a data-scaling claim for vision transfer is added.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests'/T3 and its V6 limits_scope label are overturned. The study's results bear on compute-efficiency and allocation in vision transfer, not on any version as worded. If the phenomenon file gains a vision downstream-allocation claim, rows r1 and r2 and Tables 1 and 2 could be relinked.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pre-training loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of power-law fits from smaller runs to larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their scaling with compute.
The effect of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds for visual models or other training regimes; the study reports accuracy-efficiency curves but does not fit power laws.
Predictability from pre-training loss and performance on language downstream tasks.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fit choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream segmentation performance across model sizes and pre-training FLOP budgets.
rows.measure: Downstream segmentation accuracy in the compute-efficiency comparison
rows.value: ViT-B trained with 3 × 10^18 FLOPS outperforms ViT-L trained with 6 × 10^18 FLOPS; described as a 3× gain in efficiency.
rows.note: The text states this comparison, but gives no numerical segmentation score for the pair. It shows that the larger model is not necessarily better at a given compute budget.
rows.check: This compute-matched comparison (CLIP ViT-B at 3e18 FLOPs beats ViT-L at 6e18) is about which model size is most efficient on a fixed budget. It does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss, so it does not bear on V6. No segmentation values are given in the text.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 (comparison as stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream segmentation accuracy-efficiency curves for two model sizes over tested compute budgets.
rows.measure: Downstream segmentation accuracy versus pre-training FLOPs
rows.value: ViT-B/16's FLOP efficiency exceeds ViT-L/16's across the tested compute regime; for most self-supervised methods, larger-model curves are on par or better, and the small- and large-model curves intersect.
rows.note: The statements summarize the reported comparison; the paper does not provide numerical curve values in the text. The larger-model advantage varies by method and compute regime.
rows.check: The row is a qualitative summary of crossing ViT-B and ViT-L efficiency curves across methods, with no numbers in the text. It concerns model-size allocation under compute for downstream vision accuracy, not predictability of downstream performance, and no power-law form is fitted. Its subject also mixes several methods under one row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: CLIP on JFT and the reported model-size comparisons on JFT
reader_labels.reason: Downstream accuracy-efficiency does not uniformly favor larger models: the CLIP ViT-B run at 3 × 10^18 FLOPS outperforms the ViT-L run at 6 × 10^18 FLOPS, while self-supervised size curves are described as method- and budget-dependent (r1–r2).
